p.x:
I started learning English two years ago. At first, it was very difficult. I didn't know how to say simple things, and I couldn't spell many words. The letters were the same as in other languages, but the sounds were different!
Now I practise every day. In the morning, I learn five new words. I write each word in a sentence in my notebook. If I don't know what a word means, I ask my teacher. In the evening, I listen to English songs.
My teacher says that mistakes are OK. "Everyone makes mistakes when they learn a language," she says. "That's how you learn." My favourite thing is talking to tourists in my town. They are always friendly and patient with me.

Many students ask me, "How can I become fluent quickly?" There is no magic answer, but some methods work better than others.
First, don't only study grammar. Grammar is important, but you also need lots of vocabulary and useful phrases. Flashcards are a great way to remember new words, especially if you review them regularly.
Second, listen as much as you can. Watch films and series with English subtitles. This helps you learn how to pronounce words correctly and how to divide them into syllables. Don't worry about your accent; most people understand many different accents.
Third, find a conversation partner. A native speaker is ideal, but a classmate is fine too. Practise both formal and informal situations, like a job interview and a chat with a friend. Learning idioms will make you sound more natural.
Finally, don't translate everything word by word. Try to think in English. A dictionary is useful, but if you check every word, you'll never finish a book! As one bilingual student told me, "I improved when I stopped translating from my mother tongue." It is also interesting to learn about dialects: English in Scotland, India and Australia can sound very different. Some of my students now work as interpreters.

p.t: Is It Ever Too Late to Learn?
p.x:
It is often said that children learn languages more easily than adults. In one sense this is true: young children who grow up hearing two languages achieve native-like pronunciation and intonation without apparent effort. Researchers describe this process as acquisition rather than learning, because it happens naturally, without formal instruction.
Adults, however, have advantages of their own. They can grasp grammatical rules quickly, use learning strategies deliberately and draw on knowledge of their first language. Studies show that, in the early stages, adult learners often progress faster than children. Many famous polyglots began learning most of their languages after the age of twenty.
What adults typically lack is time and exposure. A child in an immersion programme hears the language for many hours a day; an adult in a weekly evening class may hear it for ninety minutes. It is therefore unsurprising that many adult learners reach a plateau at an intermediate level of proficiency, able to communicate but struggling with colloquial speech and subtle nuances of meaning.
For speakers of languages like Thai, English presents specific challenges, from consonant clusters to the gap between spelling and sound. Yet as English has become the world's lingua franca, used daily by more non-native than native speakers, the goal has shifted. Few learners now aim to sound exactly like a native speaker. Instead, they aim to communicate clearly, understanding that a literal translation of their thoughts is rarely enough, and that real fluency means expressing ideas the way English speakers naturally would.
